sources.headline: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
sources.text: Image source, EPAImage caption, Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on MondayByOlivia Ireland and Ella KiplingUpdated 18 minutes agoRussia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.""I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.Figure caption, Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine?When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled". "That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky saidTrump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.Figure caption, What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠it ⁠was “increasingly clear” ​that Russia ⁠was unwilling to accept a US-proposed ⁠ceasefire ​on ‌energy ‌strikes, as Moscow hit ‌six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday. “This is ‌what happens when Russia ​sees the prospect of higher revenues ⁠for its war ​machine,” ​he wrote ​in ​a ‌post ​on X.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said that Russia would only negotiate “seriously” under pressure, days after president Donald Trump announced a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel. “For Germany and for Europe, such a decision is out of the question,” said Merz, referring to the US-Russia diesel deal.
Nato should signal its “red lines” to Russia over sabotage attacks in Europe, the alliance’s top military commander said. “It’s important that allies continue to consult, think about how we might respond, and make sure that we message clearly and concisely to the Russians where our red lines are,” Nato commander Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw.
Russia ⁠carried ​out drone strikes on various targets ⁠in Ukraine on Monday, including on vessels ⁠carrying military cargo, ​Russia’s ‌defence ‌ministry said. The ministry said ‌it had struck three cargo vessels which it said were being used ‌to transport military cargo to Ukraine’s Black ​Sea ports - two bound for Odesa and one ⁠heading to Mykolaiv.
A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed in a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine on Monday, the authorities said. The head of the Donetsk regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said a house in the Cherkaske area was hit with cluster munitions, accusing Russia of “a deliberate attempt” to maximise civilian casualties.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, has said Russia rejects the idea of a temporary ceasefire, telling reporters that Moscow wanted a long-term peace deal instead. “In the Kremlin, both ‌President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that ​we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible ⁠to achieve it.“
Ukraine has passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, in a move expected to remove a major stumbling block to the country’s EU ambitions. Hungary had been blocking the opening of so-called negotiation “clusters” – policy areas with which EU candidates must align their laws – accusing Kyiv of failing to protect the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.
European ⁠Union foreign ministers have ⁠a ⁠clear understanding ​that now is ⁠not the moment to ease ⁠pressure on ​Russia, ‌Kaja ‌Kallas, the bloc’s ‌foreign policy chief, told reporters on Monday. “Pressure on Moscow, ‌not concessions, is the ​fastest way to end the war,” ⁠she said following ​a gathering ​of ​European foreign ministers ​in ‌Luxembourg.
EU countries back barring entry to Russians who fought in Ukraine, but need to work out how to implement the measure, Kallas added. “The political agreement is there. We just need to work out the technicalities,” she said after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
Russia presents a long-term threat to Europe regardless of the outcome of the war in Ukraine, the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency said. Warning that Moscow wanted to upend Europe’s international order, Sina Sellen, president of the BfV, said Russian-orchestrated attacks would “continue to come”.
France’s high school students will stage new protests on Tuesday, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency is reporting. A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations, which have shaken an unpopular government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit, was already “at least 30 million euros”.
An “unprecedented” cyber-attack is behind the shutdown of refrigerator units in multiple French supermarkets, according to the chief executive of Cooperative U, one of the chains affected. At least 150 Intermarche shops were targeted, along with almost 100 Cooperative U outlets, AFP reports. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, with media reporting that hackers were “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.”

sources.headline: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agreed to 'energy ceasefire'
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," the president wrote on his Truth Social network.
Trump continued: "Both parties have agreed," before urging restraint from both Kyiv and Moscow: "Do not break it!"
Zelenskyy: Energy ceasefire 'news for me'
There was ‌no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's post that the ceasefire was "news for me."
"The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins; we are ready and we will accept it," he told Axios.How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel dealTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In a social media post later, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant, leading to power outages in the capital.
The Ukrainian leader had earlier repeated his stance that Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin curbed its energy attacks.
Trump and Zelenskyy have argued this week over Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which the US president said have contributed to a global diesel shortage, rather than the Iran war.
Trump needs lower fuel prices before midterms
Trump said Friday he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia.
The controversial move was an attempt to bring down high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections next month.
However, this move undercuts fresh US sanctions Trump signed just weeks ago to further hurt Russian energy revenues funding the war.
On Sunday, a bipartisan group fo six US senators called on the Trump administarion to "immediately reverse course" and scrap the diesel deal.
The signatories included Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Republicans Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the senators said in a joint statement.European leaders rally behind Zelenskyy
Backing Zelenskyy in the Trump row, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that she "fully supported" the call for a "ceasefire that protects global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia."
"And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people's freedom," she wrote online.
On X, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country "strongly supports" Trump's call for a "sustained energy ceasefire to start now," which he said Kyiv was ready to honor "if Russia stops its attacks."
French President Emmanuel Macron said his country backs a "real energy ceasefire," but lamented that "Russia continues to refuse that."
After earlier denouncing the Trump-Putin deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he supported the energy ceasefire, in a phone call with Trump, his office said.
War abroad, soaring prices at home: is Trump in trouble?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Blackouts and refinery strikes
Russia has repeatedly struck Ukraine's power plants and transmission lines around Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa and elsewhere, to lower civilian morale, especially during the winter months.
Recently, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting major oil refineries and other facilities to curb Moscow's refining capacity and fuel supplies.
Kyiv on Sunday pressed on its campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex.
It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

sources.headline: Russia hits Ukraine gas facilities after Trump claims 'energy ceasefire'
sources.text:
A rescue worker puts out a fire at residential houses destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
Andrii Marienko/AP
hide caption
Andrii Marienko/AP
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Russia continued missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hours after President Trump claimed that Moscow had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" designed to spare energy-related infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine.
"We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities," Zelenskyy said on the social media platform X. "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump. And the message from Russia was very clear — they don't know anything about the energy ceasefire." According to Zelenskyy, a jet-powered Iranian "shahed" drone fired from Russia struck a gas production facility around midnight, while other drones struck at least five other energy-related targets. He said 33 people were reported wounded across the country.
Later on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine supported the concept of an energy ceasefire, but he called for more pressure on Russia "for de-escalation to actually succeed." "Russia must take corresponding steps. As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President," Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post. On Sunday, Trump said on his social media platform that "both parties" had agreed to the partial ceasefire, adding, "Do not break it!" He offered no details about the arrangement. But officials in Moscow appeared to show little willingness to limit strikes. Asked about the energy ceasefire on Monday, Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea as another attempt by Zelenskyy to exploit a proposed pause in the fighting to regroup and rearm. "I do not think [Zelenskyy] deserves a respite," he said. NPR asked the White House for comment on Russia's overnight strikes and what they mean for Trump's proposed ceasefire. Administration officials have yet to respond. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has often targeted civilian infrastructure, including gas and electric systems. Trump's efforts to broker a deal protecting energy infrastructure in the warring nations comes amid rising fuel prices in the U.S., following Trump's decision to go to war with Iran. Gas prices have emerged as a major challenge for Trump and his Republican allies ahead of next month's midterm election.
Last week, Trump announced a controversial plan to reduce diesel prices by reviving imports from Russia. On Sunday, however, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators released a statement calling Trump's proposal unlawful. "Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the statement said.
An injured man collects his personal belongings in front of his house destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
Andrii Marienko/AP
hide caption
Andrii Marienko/AP
Zelenskyy and many U.S. allies have supported the idea of an energy ceasefire, while condemning Trump's plan to import Russian diesel. Zelenskyy called Trump's move a "weak decision," while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday the move is "in direct opposition" to international peace efforts. In a statement Monday, Trump described his effort to partner with Russia to lower U.S. energy prices as a part of his "America First" strategy, prioritizing U.S. interests over concerns about Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "The European Union paid Russia $250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story. I made the right choice for the American People," Trump wrote. Russia's official news agency TASS confirmed Monday that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has agreed to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. in October, with monthly supplies increasing in the months ahead. "The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027," TASS reported.
While Ukrainian officials say they have so far respected Trump's call for an energy ceasefire, they did strike large data centers inside Russia operated by Yandex, a company often described as Russia's version of Google. The strike led to service outages in parts of Russia. Zelenskyy said Monday that the strikes on Yandex have also led to a drop in the number of Russian propaganda bots appearing on social media. "A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations," he said.

sources.headline: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" after criticizing Zelenskyy
sources.text:
Updated on: October 11, 2026 / 8:14 PM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
President Trump said Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed to continue striking Russian oil refineries after coming under criticism from Mr. Trump."Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Mr. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.It's unclear exactly what the ceasefire entails, and Zelenskyy told Axios after Mr. Trump's announcement that the ceasefire "was news for me." The Ukrainian president later said in a statement posted on social media that he had spoken with members of the U.S. Congress and thanked allies for their support. But he said that despite the ceasefire announcement, Russia had struck energy infrastructure in Ukraine, including a power plant in Kharkiv."Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia does," Zelenskyy said Sunday. "The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders. We are awaiting clear details of the dialogue between America and Russia — and we expect Putin to follow through on what President Trump said."CBS News has reached out to the White House for clarity on the agreement.U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney both said in separate statements Sunday that they supported an energy ceasefire. "Ukraine is ready if Russia stops its attacks," Burnham wrote on X, adding that he had spoken with Zelenskyy on Saturday. "This is the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets."
Carney expressed his "strong support" for an energy ceasefire when he spoke with Zelenskyy Sunday. However, he denounced the U.S.-Russian deal on diesel supplies, saying it undermined efforts to ensure stability in Europe and to end the war in Ukraine.Trump criticizes Zelenskyy's leadershipMr. Trump previously took aim at the Ukrainian president's leadership, suggesting Zelenskyy should be replaced and blaming him for high diesel prices. The Ukrainian president clapped back, saying Russia alone was responsible for the war in Ukraine.The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has also pushed back at Mr. Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence.
"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the media after a German-Ukrainian business forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026.
AP Photo/Dan Bashakov
Mr. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S."I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump said.U.S. Senators: "Immediately reverse course" on Russian diesel planA bipartisan group of six U.S. Senators on Sunday called for the Trump administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.Four Republican senators — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah — and Democrat Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut signed onto the statement released Sunday in protest of the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute."The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.According to an announcement from Mr. Trump on Friday, the U.S. has made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia right away, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons after that. Amid the deal, which attempts to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has also urged Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy criticized the deal and said it would help fund Russia's war in Ukraine.
Mr. Trump has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it wil l help pay for Russia's war effort.Ukraine strikes Russian data centersThe Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra."As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.
A Yandex food delivery courier rides his scooter in Moscow, Russia, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko
In Moscow, residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger."I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."Igor Mann said he went to check the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a VPN did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.Another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience."
"It's also about work," he said, adding that they also affected "healthcare, and everything else."On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said.Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday.Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized. A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

Russia strikes power plants in Ukraine despite 'energy ceasefire' announced by Trump
Copyright Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
By Gael Camba
Published on 11/10/2026 - 16:34 GMT+2•Updated 21:18
Share
Comments
Add Euronews on Google
After Donald Trump's criticism blaming Volodymyr Zelenskyy for high diesel prices, suggesting Ukraine should get a new leader, US President announced Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an 'energy ceasefire', but Russia struck Ukrainian power plants hours after the announcement.

Multiple power plants in Ukraine were struck by Russia hours after US President Donald Trump claimed an 'energy ceasefire' between the two countries.

A power plant in Kyiv was hit by a drone, leading to power outages in the capital, followed by strikes on Kharkiv's energy infrastructure.

Earlier, Donald Trump said that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote on his Truth Social network, without giving further details.

At the time, Zelenskyy said he wasn't informed of the energy ceasefire. "It was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree", Zelenskyy told Axios.

Kyiv's allies were "awaiting details" of a ceasefire on energy targets US President Donald Trump had announced. Russia hasn't confirmed any agreement.

'Awaiting details' on ceasefire

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well", Zelensky said on his Facebook page before Russia's strikes on Ukrainian power plants.

"We are awaiting details from the American side. For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace", he said.

Emmanuel Macron said France supported a "real energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia as diesel prices are at €2.25/L.

"Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure", Macron said, adding: "France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky".

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also voiced backing for Ukraine's President, saying she "fully supported the call of President Zelenskyy for a ceasefire that would protect global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia".

Canadian PM Mark Carney was more critical of this agreement, saying it undermined efforts for stability in Europe and could "provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine".

There was no immediate confirmation from Russia of an agreement, which follows an escalation in deadly attacks in the war. Its only response was strikes on Ukrainian power plants.

"If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it", Zelenskyy told Axios.

Trump suggests Ukraine should have a 'new leader'

Zelenskyy said Ukraine's people would decide whether they want a new leader for the country in response to Trump's call for Ukraine to pick a new leader.

"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader", Zelenskyy told ABC News in a televised interview, a day after Trump said Ukraine needed a new president who would agree to end the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday his country could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.

Zelensky's comment came amid a spat between Trump and the Ukrainian leader, who had denounced a US move to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

"Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it's a fair deal", Zelenskyy said in a TV interview with ABC.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well", Sybiha wrote.

The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

US President Donald Trump has sowed more confusion, announcing an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine’s Western allies.

But the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage.

Trump’s announcement on Sunday came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.

US President Donald Trump and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Photos: AFP

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said on Truth Social. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well”.

“It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” he told Warsaw Security Forum via a video link on Monday.

“If Russia doesn’t agree to energy ceasefire – we will respond.”

The Kremlin has nothing to say yet on an “energy truce” although contacts were continuing, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, according to Tass.

A police officer and a rescuer in Kyiv carry an unexploded warhead from a Shahed drone out of a school on October 1. Photo: AP

Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday that Kyiv did not “deserve” a two-month ceasefire that could enable it to hold a presidential election, which both Moscow and Washington have called for.

“I do not think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said after Kyiv on Sunday called for a 60-day halt to fighting in response to a fresh call from Trump to hold elections.

Zelensky said on Monday that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit in the latest attacks by Moscow and that “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day,” referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now used extensively by Russia.

Participants listen as Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks via a video link during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland on Monday. Photo: AFP

Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages – prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war.

More recently, Trump’s war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.

The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key Western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission.

Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal.

But that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky.

Zelensky said the diesel deal was a “weak decision”, while several of Ukraine’s European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow.

01:24

Seven US senators – including four Republicans – released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”.

Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war.

Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that “it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader”.

He said that fuel prices were rising because of the war in the Middle East and the blocked Strait of Hormuz. “Everybody understands it,” he said.

Germany’s foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to “fully support” Zelensky.

“Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government,” Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country “strongly supports President Trump’s call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now”.

In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump’s call for Zelensky to be replaced.

“I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president,” said 40-year-old Olesia Goncharuk.

“We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people,” she said.

Additional reporting by Bloomberg
